name: memory-manager
title: Memory Manager
description: What the AI remembers about a person, with scope, edit, delete and reset.
purpose: A card listing what the assistant remembers about a person, split into preferences and facts. Each memory shows its scope, when it was added and where it came from, and can be edited in place or deleted. A switch turns memory off and says what stops, and one reset action clears everything behind a confirmation. A small chip, exported separately, tells the person in the conversation that a memory was just saved.
whyItMatters: Memory is only trusted when it can be inspected. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity and Apple each let a person see saved memories, but they differ on whether a memory shows its source, whether work and personal sets are told apart, and how a wipe is confirmed. Shape of AI's memory pattern asks for the same things this component builds in: visible provenance, scope you can read, per-item control, and a capture moment that does not happen silently.
usage: Pass `memories` and own them: the component calls `onEdit(id, text)`, `onDelete(id)` and `onReset()` and you update the list. Give each memory a `scope`, either `"global"` or `{ workspace }`, and pass `activeWorkspace` when the person has more than one memory set so rows held for another workspace say they are not used. Set `source` whenever you know it. Control `enabled` with `onEnabledChange`. When the assistant saves something, render `MemorySavedChip` in the conversation with an `onReview` that opens this card, and pass the new item's id as `justSavedId` so the row is marked. Training and retention belong in data-controls, and a session that remembers nothing belongs in private-session-notice.

anatomy.note: The card. A named group, so a screen reader announces the section.
Card title. A heading whose level you set with `headingLevel`; focus moves here after a delete.
Turns memory on or off. Described by the statement beside it.
One sentence on what happens now, and what stops when the switch is off.
Names private sessions in copy. It renders no notice.
One group, Preferences or Facts, with a labelled header and count.
The remembered sentence. It names the row's buttons.
Scope, date added and source, as text. Beside the row, not inside it, so it never truncates.
Opens the in-place editor for this row.
Deletes this row only. Calls `onDelete` with its id.
The editing form: a labelled textarea with Save and Cancel.
Opens the reset confirmation. Absent when nothing is saved.
Alert dialog saying what is deleted and what is kept. `onReset` fires from its confirm button only.
Visually hidden live region for saves, deletes and resets.
The capture-moment chip, a separate export you place in the chat.
Calls `onReview`. Only present when you pass the handler.

variants.none: No variant axis: the seven states are driven by the data and the host, through memories, scope, enabled and the justSavedId, defaultEditingId and defaultResetOpen props.

insteadUse.when: The choice is about training on conversations or how long they are retained. That is data handling by the provider, not what the assistant recalls about the person.
You need to tell the person this session remembers nothing. Memory-manager only mentions private sessions in one sentence of copy.
You need the whole settings surface with navigation and many sections. Memory-manager is one section's worth and lives inside that surface.
The person is managing their own files and uploads. Memory-manager holds what the assistant inferred, not what the person stored.

dos: Show scope, date and source on every row, as text, so no memory is a black box.
Edit in place with a labelled field and Save/Cancel, so the person corrects a memory without deleting and re-teaching it.
Tell the person in the conversation when a memory is saved, with a way to review it.
Put reset behind a confirmation that says what it deletes and what it keeps.
donts: Don't list memories as bare sentences. Without a date, a source and a scope, nobody can judge whether to keep one.
Don't offer a Clear button that acts at once and does not say what it removes.
Don't mix preferences and facts in one pile. How the assistant should write and who the person is get reviewed differently.

keyboard: Tab stops in order: the memory switch, then for each row Edit and Delete, then Reset all memories. Space toggles the switch; Enter or Space activates a button.
In the editor the textarea takes focus on open; Tab reaches Save then Cancel. Enter inside the textarea adds a new line, so Save is the button. Escape cancels the edit and does nothing else.
Save is natively disabled while the field is empty, which removes it from the tab order.

The reset dialog traps focus, Escape closes it without calling `onReset`, and the confirm button is the only way to fire it. The component does not set `disabled` anywhere else; there is no prop that disables the whole card.
screenReader: The card is a `group` named by its title, and the title is a heading at the level you pass in `headingLevel`. Each memory group is a labelled section whose name includes its count.

Edit and Delete are named by their own text plus the memory sentence through `aria-labelledby`, so a list of buttons reads "Delete Use British spelling in documents." rather than ten identical "Delete" buttons. A very long memory makes a long name.
The switch is named "Memory" and described by the statement, so the sentence saying what stops is read with the control.
Dates are `time` elements with a machine-readable value; scope and source are plain text, never a colour or an icon alone.

Saves, deletes and resets are announced through one polite status region. The switch announces its own new state; the changed statement beside it is not in a live region and is read only when the person moves to it.

`MemorySavedChip` is `role="status"`, so it is announced when it is inserted. Insert it fresh; one that is already on the page when it first renders is not announced. Its review button is named "Review" plus the chip label.
focus: Opening the editor moves focus to the textarea. Save or Cancel returns focus to that row's Edit button.
Delete and a confirmed reset move focus to the card title, because the row or the Reset button they came from is gone. Cancelling a dialog opened from the Reset button returns focus to that button.

pitfalls: Not updating `memories` in the handlers. The component is controlled: `onEdit`, `onDelete` and `onReset` only report the request, so a handler that does nothing leaves the list unchanged.
Rendering `MemorySavedChip` inside this card. It belongs in the conversation, at the moment of capture; the card only marks the row with `justSavedId`.
Passing a local-time string as `addedAt` and expecting local dates. Dates are shown as calendar dates in UTC so the text is identical on every machine; pass an ISO date.
Putting training or retention controls in this card. They govern the provider's data use, not what the assistant recalls about the person; use data-controls for them.
Expecting `enabled={false}` to hide or disable the list. Saved memories stay visible and editable while memory is off, because the person must still be able to delete them.

Pairing `text-muted-foreground` with a muted, accent or secondary surface when you wrap the card. The rows are written for the card surface; if you paint the wrapper, rebind `--muted-foreground` on it.
